authoring_notes: AUTHORING PROVENANCE. Every expected value here was derived from the canonical protocol-v2 record and the repository's security and product contracts. The settled v2 surface avoids v1 shapes such as the `pipe.expose` name, the `target: "ip:port"` string, `opened_by`, `authorized_peer`, `state: open|closed`, `local_addr`, `pipe_denied`, `peer_unreachable`, and `invalid_params`; its canonical pipe.list row is `{pipe_id, published_by, device_id, published_at, link, connected}`.

STEP VOCABULARY (extensions to the v1 harness, all language-neutral). `as` names the actor: A = room authority/publisher, B = active non-authority member, D = a second member used for audience scoping, C = a subject with no membership, A2 = a second authenticated session principal on A's daemon. `in` is the request payload. `expect` is SUBSET-matched (extra keys allowed) because this corpus fixes only what the spec forces; forbidden keys are asserted explicitly with the `<absent>` tag, which means the key MUST NOT be present at all. `expect_error.fields` is likewise subset-matched with `<absent>` available. `save_error` captures a whole error object for later comparison. `harness` steps are setup/fault-injection actions, not protocol operations. `check` steps make cross-step assertions and issue no call. `assert` keys used: no_null_values, identical_to, errors_identical, errors_identical_modulo, timing_indistinguishable, not_equal, greater_than, array_len, strictly_increasing, code_not, codes_equal, host_is_loopback, distinct_keys, equal_modulo.

TYPE TAGS. Reused from the v1 harness: `<hex64>`, `<room_id>`, `<ts>`, `<number>`. Added: `<pipe_id>` and `<connection_id>` (deliberately OPAQUE — the spec fixes no lexical form, so the harness must accept any non-empty scalar and the corpus must not pin v1's 32-hex spelling), `<port>` (integer 1..=65535), `<loopback_host>` (an IP literal inside 127.0.0.0/8 or ::1), `<pos>` (a per-room monotonic push position), `<any>` (present, type unconstrained), `<absent>` (key MUST NOT be present).

SETTLED PIPE LIST FACTS. `link` is the publisher-device reachability fact and `connected` is the local-daemon connection fact. They remain separately named fields with different scopes; neither an invented `reachability` wrapper nor an invented `local_connection` variant exists.

SETTLED LINK STATES. Pipe rows reuse the canonical `link` domain used by peers and file providers. A lack of route is `not_connected{reason}`; revocation is not a link state because revoked pipes are omitted from pipe.list.
SETTLED TARGET REFUSAL. `target` is `{host, port}`. A malformed target is `invalid_argument`; a syntactically valid non-loopback target is `pipe_target_refused` carrying that target verbatim.

SETTLED AUTHORIZATION. `pipe.publish` is open to every active member; only the record's four authority-gated operations require authority. `pipe.revoke` is restricted to the publisher and answers `pipe_not_publisher` for another member; outside-audience connect answers `pipe_unknown`.

SETTLED PIPE ERRORS. The canonical operation-specific codes include `pipe_unknown`, `pipe_unreachable`, `pipe_revoked`, `pipe_not_publisher`, and `connection_unknown`, with the field sets pinned by the operation tables and taxonomy.

GAP I COULD NOT CLOSE — pipe.list has no read-specific error code. It is a pure room-scoped read whose only failure modes are preconditions, so its most specific code is `room_not_available`, which it shares with every other room-scoped operation. That satisfies "not a generic invalid_argument" but not, strictly, "its own" code. The spec's rule that every operation has at least one code specific to it may require jeliya-api to add one (or to concede that read operations are exempt). Flagging rather than inventing one.

GAP — no served limit bounds pipes. The limits object has no max_pipes, max_pipe_connections, or equivalent, so there is no pipes-domain `resource_exhausted{resource, limit}` case that reads a served bound. My boundary cases therefore sit on the two bounds that ARE determinate: the edge of the loopback block (127.255.255.254 in / 128.0.0.1 out, plus ::1) and the 16-bit port range (65535 in / 65536 and 0 out). If a pipe or forwarding-session limit is later served, a matching at-limit / one-past pair must be added, because an unbounded number of loopback listeners is a real daemon resource.

AMBIGUITY — pipe.release addressing. Release names a `connection_id`, not a `pipe_id`, because the spec makes release a distinct operation from revoke and describes it as releasing "a local connection"; with two connections to one pipe, a pipe-keyed release would tear down a sibling. I also require `room` on release so the accepted-room guard runs uniformly (security-threat-model.md's authorization invariant), and a mismatched (room, connection_id) pair answers `connection_unknown` — never confirming the connection exists under another room.

SETTLED REVOCATION VISIBILITY. A successful revoke removes the pipe from pipe.list because the canonical row has no revocation variant and the closed-pipe projection filters it. Operations that still name the retired pipe surface `pipe_revoked`; a refused non-publisher revoke leaves the publication listed unchanged.

AMBIGUITY — push frame naming. The record names only the `gap` and `peer` frames, so I did NOT invent a `pipe.*` push name. The ordering and boundary cases assert only what the spec fixes about ANY push — `t` present, `id` absent, a `room`, and a strictly increasing gap-free per-room `pos` — and select frames by "names this pipe_id". The release-vs-revoke case deliberately uses B's converged `pipe.list` as its observable rather than a push name, so it is airtight regardless of how the frame is spelled. Only the U1 case names `peer`, which the record itself names.

AMBIGUITY — the no-subject precondition code. The record removes the pre-identity carve-out ("one precondition, two answers") but does not spell the surviving answer. I pinned `subject_absent`, matching hello's `subject: {state: absent}` variant and v2's identity→subject renaming. The case is written so it still catches the real regression if the spelling differs: it asserts the code is IDENTICAL across pipe.list, room.members, and fleet.list, is not `room_not_available` or `invalid_argument`, and that no surface answers an empty success result.

ORDERING SEMANTICS. The ordering case asserts strict increase and contiguity WITHIN one room only, and explicitly asserts nothing about ordering relative to any other room, because the record states no cross-room ordering exists and a client must not infer one. A fixture that pinned interleaving across rooms would be asserting a fact v2 declines to provide.

op_id COVERAGE. All four mutating pipe operations are on the op_id-deduplicated list, so every one has a replay case asserting the ORIGINAL result and no second effect. Three ledger properties from the record are also covered: it survives reconnection (publish), it is keyed on (session principal, op_id) so two principals on one daemon do not collide (publish), and a malformed op_id is rejected before any effect. The record says mutating operations "accept" an op_id but does not say whether omitting it is an error, so no fixture asserts a missing-op_id behaviour — that is an open question for jeliya-api.

NON-ORACLE COVERAGE. All five pipe operations are room-scoped, so the dedicated non-oracle case exercises all five against a real-but-foreign room and a never-existed room and asserts byte-identical errors plus indistinguishable timing. A second case covers the pipe-level oracle the room-level one misses: a genuine pipe_id from room X presented against room Y answers `pipe_unknown` exactly as a fabricated id does, so a member of an unrelated room cannot confirm a foreign pipe exists. Both assert `hint` is absent.
